question.problem: Find and categorize all local the extrema of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x+4,$ and determine which of the following statements is true.
question.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, we compute the first derivative of $f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x+4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x+4)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x-4 & 6y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2x-4=0 \\ 6y=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $x,$ we get

$$
2x-4=0\,⟹\,x=2.
$$

Solving the second equation for $y,$ we get

$$
6y=0\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

Hence, $(2,0)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

To classify this stationary point, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-4)=2\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6y)=0 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-4)=0\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6y)=6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(2,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2,0)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(2,0),$ we get

$$
H(2,0)=det({f}^{″}(2,0))=2\cdot 6-{0}^{2}=12>0.
$$

Finally, notice that 

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(2,0)=({f}^{″}(2,0))_{11}=2>0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum at $(2,0).$
